extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Ravi Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Working through textbook material and exercises on differentials, cotangent bundles, Hodge theory, ramification, and the Riemann–Hurwitz formula in algebraic geometry (Vakil's 'The Rising Sea').

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler exact sequence for projective bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a rank n+1 locally free sheaf on a scheme X and π: P_V → X is the corresponding projective bundle, then the relative cotangent sheaf fits into an Euler exact sequence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated: 0 → Ω_{P_V/X} → π^*V^∨ ⊗ O_{P_V}(-1) → O_{P_V} → 0. The text notes this generalizes the usual Euler sequence for projective space and is useful (e.g., for P^1-bundles over curves, Exercise 20.2.J). No proof is given here but the sequence is asserted to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassmannian universal sequence and cotangent identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Over the Grassmannian G(m,n+1) there is a canonical short exact sequence 0 → S → O_{G} ⊗ V^∨ → Q → 0 (S the tautological subbundle, Q the quotient), and a canonical isomorphism Ω_{G(m,n+1)/k} ≅ Hom(Q,S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a generalization of the Euler sequence; Exercise 21.4.I asks to prove the identification and relate it to the m=1/projective-space case. The text indicates further generalizations to Grassmannian bundles and flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of i-forms (relative i-forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism X → Y, the sheaf of relative i-forms is defined as Ω^i_{X/Y} := ∧^i Ω_{X/Y}; sections over an open set are called relative i-forms over that open set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic object used to define invariants like geometric genus and Hodge numbers; a brief joke and exercises follow to build intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birational invariance of H^0(X, Ω^i)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and X' are birational irreducible smooth projective k-varieties then for each i, H^0(X, Ω^i_{X/k}) ≅ H^0(X', Ω^i_{X'/k}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook gives a hint: fix a birational map φ: X --→ X'; the complement of the domain has codimension ≥ 2 (Exercise 15.3.C); pull back forms on the domain and extend using Algebraic Hartogs (12.3.14) and the fact that Ω^i is locally free. Exercise 21.5.A asks to verify this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical bundle and geometric genus
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-dimensional smooth k-variety X, the canonical (line) bundle is K_X := det Ω_{X/k} = Ω^n_{X/k}. The geometric genus is pg(X) := h^0(X, K_X) = h^0(X, Ω^n_{X/k}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links K_X to the dualizing sheaf and Serre duality (Miracle 18.5.2) and uses pg(X) as a birational invariant for projective smooth varieties (see Exercise 21.5.A). Further exercises explore adjunction and examples (curves, surfaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction formula for canonical bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a smooth variety and Z ⊂ X a smooth subvariety, then K_Z ≅ (K_X|_Z) ⊗ det N_{Z/X}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For codimension 1 this specializes to K_Z ≅ (K_X ⊗ O_X(Z))|_Z (often written K_X(Z)|_Z). Exercise 21.5.B asks to prove this (hint: apply Exercise 14.2.X to Theorem 21.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of jth plurigenus and Kodaira dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth projective k-variety X, the jth plurigenus is P_j(X) := h^0(X, K_X^{⊗ j}). The Kodaira dimension κ(X) is the smallest k such that P_j / j^k is bounded as j varies through positive integers; if all P_j = 0, then κ(X) = -1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states the plurigenera are birational invariants (Exercise 21.5.D), and gives remarks about existence of κ(X) and its relation to pluricanonical rational maps (references given). Exercises connect Kodaira dimension to being of general type (κ(X)=dim X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification labels: Fano / Calabi–Yau / general type (for smooth projective varieties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The textbook introduces the three important classes: 'Fano', 'Calabi–Yau', and 'general type' for smooth projective k-varieties, relating these to properties of the canonical bundle K_X and its positivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises illustrate the trichotomy in dimension 1 (curves): genus 0 → Fano, genus 1 → Calabi–Yau, genus >1 → general type (Exercise 21.5.F). Exercise 21.5.G works out the canonical bundle for complete intersections and classifies when they fall into these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kodaira vanishing theorem (statement and hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k has characteristic 0 and X is a smooth projective k-variety, then for any ample invertible sheaf L, Hi(X, K_X ⊗ L) = 0 for i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes the characteristic-0 restriction (Raynaud counterexamples exist in positive characteristic) and sketches provenance of proofs (analytic via GAGA, reductions to C, Lefschetz principle, and algebraic proofs via positive characteristic methods). Exercise 21.5.J asks to prove special cases (dim 1 and P^n_k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Hodge numbers and basic invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth projective variety X, the Hodge numbers are h^{i,j}(X) := dim H^j(X, Ω^i_{X/k}). In particular h^{i,0} are birational invariants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming miracle 18.5.2 (canonical bundle Serre-dualizing), Serre duality gives symmetry h^{p,q} = h^{n-p,n-q} (Exercise 21.5.K). Over C one has the Hodge decomposition H^m(X,C) = ⊕_{i+j=m} H^j(X, Ω^i_{X/C}), yielding the additional symmetry h^{i,j} = h^{j,i} (21.5.11). Several exercises ask to compute Hodge diamonds for projective space and products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal automorphisms and deformations (cohomological interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a variety X, H^0(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal automorphisms and H^1(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal deformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the example P^1: T_{P^1} ≅ O(2) so h^0(P^1, T_{P^1}) = 3 equals the dimension of Aut(P^1) (Exercise 15.2.D). Exercises ask to compute h^i(C, T_C) for curves of genus g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unramified and formally unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y, the support of Ω_π := Ω_{X/Y} is the ramification locus. If Ω_π = 0 then π is formally unramified; if in addition π is locally of finite type then π is unramified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions that some authors replace 'locally of finite type' with 'locally of finite presentation' and that definitions may vary slightly (EGA reference). Numerous exercises explore examples and equivalent characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples of unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally closed embeddings are unramified; localization maps Spec S^{-1}B → Spec B are formally unramified; finite separable field extensions (viewed as maps of schemes) are unramified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.6.A lists these as easy checks. The generic point inclusion Spec O_{Y,η} → Spec Y is formally unramified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiberwise characterization of unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is unramified iff for each point q ∈ Y, the fiber π^{-1}(q) is (scheme-theoretically) a disjoint union of copies of Spec K where K is a finite separable extension of κ(q). Equivalently, after base-change to geometric points, the fiber is a disjoint union of copies of the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Exercise 21.6.D and provides a concrete geometric/fiberwise test for unramifiedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of unramified morphisms via diagonal/embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: For a locally finite type morphism π: X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes, π is unramified iff the diagonal morphism δ_π: X → X ×_Y X is a closed embedding with ideal sheaf I satisfying I = I^2, which forces δ_π to be an open embedding (hence an immersion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.6.F gives the argument (Nakayama's lemma, support considerations) and asks to generalize dropping Noetherian hypotheses by working with finitely presentedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and openness properties of unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If τ = π ◦ ρ and τ is unramified then π is unramified; if ρ is unramified and τ is smooth of relative dimension n then π is smooth of relative dimension n. The locus in X where π is unramified is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.6.G and 21.6.H ask to check these composition and openness properties; geometric intuition is suggested (e.g., tangent-vector criterion for injectivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic interpretation: different and discriminant
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is the ring of integers in a number field, the different ideal of B is the annihilator of Ω_{B/Z}; it measures how (un)ramified Spec B → Spec Z is. The discriminant ideal corresponds to the pushforward of the different divisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an arithmetic side remark (21.6.1). The textbook notes these are ring-theoretic versions of ramification loci and will not be used further here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: separable (finite) morphism between integral schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite morphism between integral schemes X → Y is separable if it is dominant and the induced extension of function fields K(X)/K(Y) is separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generically finite morphisms are called generically separable under the analogous condition. The text observes finite morphisms are automatically separable in characteristic 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left-exactness of the cotangent sequence for generically separable maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is generically separable between irreducible smooth varieties of the same dimension n, then the cotangent exact sequence is exact on the left:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated: 0 → π^*Ω_{Y/k} → Ω_{X/k} → Ω_{X/Y} → 0 (Proposition 21.7.2). The proof reduces to checking injectivity at the generic point where separability implies Ω_{K(X)/K(Y)} = 0, so the map of rank-n vector spaces is injective; torsion-freeness of locally free sheaves on integral schemes is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local description of ramification in dimension 1 (curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a point p of X lying over q of Y (both regular points on regular curves), writing a uniformizer relation t = u s^n (u unit) gives dt = u n s^{n-1} ds + s^n du; dt vanishes to order at least n−1. If that order equals n−1 (and n not divisible by char), the ramification is tame; if greater, it is wild. The ramification index is defined as one plus this vanishing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.B asks to relate the degree of Ω_{X/Y} at p to the ramification order minus one. This local calculation motivates the definitions of tame/wild ramification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch divisor multiplicity via number of preimages (tame case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all ramification above q ∈ Y is tame (always true in characteristic 0), then the multiplicity of the branch divisor at q equals deg π − |π^{-1}(q)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.C explains that the branch divisor measures how the number of preimages is less than the degree (counted with multiplicity); Figure 21.4 illustrates an example where branch multiplicity is 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Hurwitz formula (curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a finite separable morphism of projective regular curves of pure degree n and R is the ramification divisor, then 2g(X) − 2 = n(2g(Y) − 2) + deg R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook states this as Theorem 21.7.3 and suggests proving it by applying additivity of degree in exact sequences to the left-exact cotangent sequence (21.7.2.1) and interpreting deg R as h^0(Ω_{X/Y}) (Exercise 21.7.D). Several corollaries and applications are given (bounds on branch points, discriminant degree calculation, Lüröth's theorem, automorphism group bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and applications of Riemann–Hurwitz
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications include: the degree of the ramification divisor is always even; Lüröth's theorem (if g(X)=0 then subfields of k(x) containing k are of the form k(f(x))); bounds on automorphism groups of curves via Riemann–Hurwitz (Hurwitz bound |Aut(C)| ≤ 84(g−1) in characteristic 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 21.7.4–21.7.M develop these consequences: Example that any cover of a curve must be branched over an even number of points; using Riemann–Hurwitz to bound automorphism groups (21.7.9–21.7.M) via analysis of branch points and ramification indices.
